title: Otis Cloud EMS 2.0
subtitle: Turning a legacy monitoring system into a proactive, cloud-native platform — by designing for fear, not just efficiency

meta.label: Team
meta.value: 2 UI Designers · 10+ Engineers · 1 PM · 1 Project Manager

meta.label: Recognition
meta.value: 2026 Red Dot Award: Brands & Communication Design

value: Otis's clients manage complex properties worldwide, but legacy on-premise infrastructure made real-time equipment monitoring nearly impossible. That opacity forced reactive maintenance — waiting for elevators to fail before fixing them — driving up downtime, cost, and friction. The hypothesis: real-time health data and predictive alerts could cut emergency repair calls by 20% and lift satisfaction.

I was brought in as Lead Designer to move this rigid system to a cloud-native, globally scalable ecosystem. But the mandate arrived as a slogan — "move our legacy system to the cloud, and make it scale globally" — with no user, no scenario, and no definition of success. "Cloud" is a technical action, not a user need.
So my first move wasn't visual. It was turning the slogan back into a question that could be answered.

items.label: Constraint 1
items.title: Bridging the technical gap
items.desc: "Power user" tools for technical experts — without overwhelming non-technical stakeholders.

items.label: Constraint 2
items.title: High-stakes compliance
items.desc: User-centricity inside rigid safety and data regulations.

items.label: Constraint 3
items.title: Global diversity
items.desc: A "universal" system that still respects local market nuances.

indexedSections.title: Four moves from slogan to problem

blocks.title: Strip the solution back to the problem

value: When I aligned with the business and PM, the "requirement" was crisp and specific: "We need a real-time monitoring dashboard." Classic solution-as-requirement. So instead of taking the order, I traced it back with a few whys: Why real-time monitoring? Because clients can't see equipment health. Why is that a problem? Because if they can't see it, they can only fix elevators after they break — reactive maintenance: expensive, disruptive, and a constant source of complaints.

items.label: The actual problem
items.desc: Clients are trapped in a reactive firefighting model — and can't move to proactive prevention.

blocks.value: That single reframe — from "build a dashboard" to "move clients from reactive firefighting to proactive prevention" — set the direction for everything that followed.

blocks.label: 5-whys trace — from "we need a dashboard" down to "trapped in reactive firefighting"

blocks.title: Go to the field — every need I had was second-hand

value: Before committing, I hit the brakes on one realization: every "user need" I had was second-hand. The information reaching HQ in New York had been relayed through sales, support, and engineering — several layers of distortion. The users described in a conference room and the ones standing in an actual machine room could easily be two different people. I couldn't even follow their vocabulary — car call, hall call, group dispatch.

With no dedicated researcher and a lean team (me + 2 UI designers), a months-long study was off the table. So I chose the lowest-cost path to the highest-fidelity truth: on-site contextual inquiry at several high-traffic properties in NYC — standing behind users, watching them operate the system for real.

blocks.label: Field visit — the front-desk workstation at One Columbus Circle, where the legacy system actually lives

value: The field flipped our assumptions. Everyone — myself included — had assumed users wanted efficiency, to go faster. What I actually saw was that non-technical building managers were operating in fear.
One manager stuck with me. For a trivial operation, he'd rather phone an Otis engineer than press the button himself. When I asked why, he said:

blocks.value: I'm afraid I'll shut down every elevator in the building.

That was the moment. We were designing for efficiency — but users were stuck in fear. I named it consequence anxiety: the dread of an irreversible, catastrophic mistake. That anxiety made them offload even the simplest tasks to engineers — which meant our backend usage data was a false positive. The real pain point was invisible in the data; it only surfaced on-site.

blocks.label: The trap
blocks.value: Usage data looked healthy because engineers were doing the work managers feared to touch. The metric wasn't measuring adoption — it was measuring avoidance.

value: The hard part: fear doesn't fit in a PRD, and engineers can't sprint-plan an emotion. So my final discovery move was to translate the feeling into concrete, testable design requirements. I codified "users operate in fear" into a design principle — psychological safety before efficiency — and broke it into three things engineering could actually build and validate:

items.title: Strong confirmation
items.desc: High-consequence, irreversible actions require explicit, informed confirmation.

items.title: Safe defaults
items.desc: The risky path is the deliberate one — never the accidental one.

items.title: Plain-language labels
items.desc: Jargon like "car call" replaced with words a non-expert understands — field testing showed unlabeled car vs. hall call types caused pure guesswork.

blocks.value: To hold the team to one axis, I defined two lean personas around the core tension — Action vs. Oversight:

items.label: Action
items.title: Field Engineer
items.desc: Highly technical, occasional user diagnosing issues on-site. Needs real-time status, high-density actionable data, and predictable workflows with minimal friction.

items.label: Oversight
items.title: Building Manager
items.desc: Non-technical daily user managing operations and tenant communication. Needs guided workflows, plain-language labels, and confirmation before committing changes.

blocks.value: For the first time, the business goals — cloud, adoption, cost reduction — and the user goal — don't let me make a catastrophic mistake — were aligned into a single definition of success.

indexedSections.title: From insight to a shippable system

blocks.value: With the problem correctly framed, execution followed a phased, de-risked path: discovery and quick wins first — low-risk UX improvements to build stakeholder confidence — then validation and workflow cleanup, then beta and a longer-term AI vision.

blocks.label: Four phases — Discovery & Research, Testing & Validation, Beta Test & Launch, Future Vision

items.title: Dashboard & AI Copilot
items.desc: Real-time service visibility, with the "Ask Otis" copilot surfacing insights and guiding next steps while keeping users in control.

items.title: Traffic Control & Monitoring
items.desc: Modular tools for security teams and engineers to manage calls, secure floors, and schedule elevator operations in real time.

items.title: Health & Energy
items.desc: AI-powered insights that surface early risks, predict maintenance needs, and cut energy consumption.

items.title: New User Guide
items.desc: Guided onboarding with contextual tutorials that shorten training time and build confidence faster.

blocks.label: Cloud EMS dashboard — plain-language labels, safe defaults, Ask Otis one click away
"Ask Otis" AI Copilot — guided insights in context

blocks.value: With my two UI designers I extended the design system with the reusable pieces the old platform never had — a full charting library and a plain-spoken empty-state and iconography set — so "safe and legible" scaled beyond the screens I touched personally.

blocks.label: Design system — charting library built for the new analytics surfaces
Design system — empty states in plain language

blocks.value: Then I proved the reframe: confirmation-and-default patterns tested against the consequence-anxiety hypothesis with real users, inside active sprint cycles — decisions grounded in measured performance, not assumptions.

blocks.label: Remote usability sessions on the Cloud EMS prototype
Before/after results board — completion time, completion rate, and errors per task, with pain-point notes

indexedSections.title: From dreaded chore to daily tool

value: Cloud EMS 2.0 launched in early September — modernizing elevator management across 10+ core workflows and three user roles, and automating complex edge cases to reduce operational burden.

Beyond the numbers, the real shift was behavioral: building managers began operating the system themselves, no longer defaulting to Otis engineers for routine work. The platform went from a dreaded chore to a high-velocity tool — and earned a Red Dot Award. The success became the mandate for my next strategic initiative: reimagining enterprise security controls.

indexedSections.title: The real requirement isn't in the doc

value: The most valuable lesson: the real requirement is rarely in the requirements doc — it lives in the behavior users won't say out loud, or don't even notice themselves.

blocks.value: My job is to dig the real requirement out of the ambiguity, translate it into something a whole team can build against, and align everyone to it.
